sources.title: Quapaw Nation, O-ga-xpa Ma-zhoⁿ: Quapaw Country
sources.note: Pages 1 to 10 and 16 to 17: tribal-authored homeland account, debated chronology, O-ga-xpa name, villages, seasonal life, trade, disease, removals, dispersal, and continuity.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Tribal Name Origin and History
sources.note: Sections “The Downstream People” and “Language Comparison”: Quapaw oral history, Ogaxpa as downstream people, and documented spelling variants.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, The Quapaw Indians
sources.note: Lines 123 to 135 and accompanying sections: documented colonial-era food, clothing, family, clans, houses, village councils, ceremonies, diplomacy, and forced cessions.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, The Osotouy Project
sources.note: Lines 107 to 124: collaborative archaeology, site setting, GIS and remote sensing across five hectares, probable structure, trash pits, pottery, animal bone, and feasting evidence.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, Feature 12 at Wallace Bottom
sources.note: Lines 112 to 129: likely colonial-period Quapaw village context, eighteenth-century midden, Native pottery, antler points, daub, French objects, fauna, and interpretive limits.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Menard-Hodges Site
sources.note: Sections on landscape, chronology, mound and plaza layout, uncertain Osotouy location, children’s graves, later remote sensing, habitation debris, preservation, and looting damage.

sources.title: National Park Service, Arkansas Post Timeline: Prehistory to 1763
sources.note: Timeline entries for lower Arkansas archaeology, mid-sixteenth-century Quapaw residence, 1673 visitors, 1686 post, missions, alliance, warfare, flooding, and imperial transfer.

sources.title: National Park Service, Arkansas Post Timeline: Spanish Domain, 1763 to 1804
sources.note: Timeline entries for Spanish rule, Quapaw diplomacy, repeated floods, the 1779 relocation, and the 1783 Colbert Raid attack on Arkansas Post.

sources.title: National Park Service, Parts I and II Cultural Landscape Report: Arkansas Post National Memorial - Gillett, Arkansas
sources.note: Official NPS DataStore record 2185887 for the 2005 report; report page 74 discusses the 1779 map, thirty-five Quapaw houses east of the Post, rounded dwellings, likely fields or gardens, paths, and a source-qualified reconstruction.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, The Calumet Ceremony in the Mississippi Valley
sources.note: Document exercise using 1673, 1701, and 1727 missionary accounts to explain welcome, kinship, reciprocity, obligation, and cross-cultural misunderstanding.

sources.title: United States Statutes at Large, Treaty with the Quapaws, 1818
sources.note: Printed pages 176 to 178, especially Articles 2 to 5: vast land cession, retained tract, conditional hunting, settlement restrictions, and payments in goods.

sources.title: United States Statutes at Large, Treaty with the Quapaws, 1824
sources.note: Printed pages 232 to 234, especially Articles 1 to 5: remaining Arkansas cession, farm losses, annuities, imposed removal, and promised travel provisions.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation Language Department, official homepage
sources.note: Heading “Hawé, Welcome!” and current teaching notices: official language resources, curriculum, historical documents, dictionary work, and introductory-speech classes.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation Language Department, About Our Website
sources.note: Sections “Our Purpose” and “Dhegiha Language Resources”: archive dates, dormancy, no living fluent speakers, revitalization, related but distinct languages, and community authorship.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation Language Department, Okáxpa Pronunciation Guide
sources.note: Overview, glossary, and phoneme table: current IPA-based writing, ogonek nasal vowels, stress marks, consonants, and securely glossed modern examples.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation Language Department, Valentine’s Day in Okáxpa
sources.note: Post dated 3 February 2025: department-authored phrase Ąkoža tteá, translated “let’s (you and I) dance,” with grammar and modern cultural context.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation Language Department, Updates and News
sources.note: 2025 and 2026 notices: classes, shared meals, online prayer course, and a workshop studying a fluent speaker’s story transcribed in the 1890s.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Anthropological Archives, Guide to MS 4800 James O. Dorsey papers
sources.note: Finding aid printed pages 80 to 81, box 41A, items 278 to 287: Quapaw vocabulary dated 1883, 1890, and 1894, plus dated Kwapa texts and linguistic notes.

sources.title: Quapaw Tribal Ancestry, Quapaw Stories and Interviews
sources.note: Community archive of 1960s and 1969 to 1970 interviews covering family history, foot races, food, dance, naming, herbs, education, burial, language, and teaching young people.

sources.title: Quapaw Tribal Ancestry, Quapaw Clans
sources.note: Community research page explains paternal clan or gens membership and attributes twenty-three recorded groups to Dorsey interviews around 1890.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Governing Resolution
sources.note: Official summary dates the governing resolution to 19 August 1956 and describes elected institutional authority and later membership legislation.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Education
sources.note: Current official education page lists college, vocational, dual-credit, graduation, internship, camp, and scholarship information for Quapaw citizens.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Community Health Program
sources.note: Responsibilities and policy sections: home visits, health education, medication help, screenings, transport, wound care, sanitation teaching, and culturally responsive current care.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Environmental Department
sources.note: Mission and programs: human health, cultural heritage, water and air quality, solid and hazardous waste, recycling, Tar Creek oversight, monitoring, and community education.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Business Committee
sources.note: Official page states the Business Committee was established in 1956 and describes seven elected members serving staggered terms.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, Indians in Arkansas: The Quapaw Indians
sources.note: PDF sections on documented colonial-era houses, village councils, clothing, ceremonies, families and clans, food, diplomacy, and the limits of later descriptions.

sources.title: Theodore Catton, A Many-Storied Place: Historic Resource Study, Arkansas Post National Memorial, Arkansas
sources.note: 2017 report, chapter 2, “The Site in Antiquity and Quapaw Ethnogenesis,” especially printed page 64 and the surrounding discussion: competing models, Menard and Wallace Bottom, consultation, and caution about prematurely naming an archaeological phase Quapaw.

sources.title: National Park Service, Arkansas: Arkansas Post National Memorial
sources.note: Sections on repeated Arkansas Post relocations, proximity to a Quapaw village, Chickasaw conflict, French military planning, flooding, later Spanish trade, and the 1783 defense.

sources.title: Quapaw Nation, Saracen
sources.note: Official biography sections on 1818 and 1824 cessions, 1826 removal, Red River flooding and disease, returns to Arkansas, delayed payments and hunger, the 1833 treaty, kin memory, and documentary uncertainty.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Arkansas, Smallpox
sources.note: Section on Indigenous Arkansas: documented Quapaw smallpox epidemic around 1698, sharply reduced population estimates, and caution about unsupported disease projections into earlier periods.

sources.title: Marvin D. Jeter et al., Archeology and Bioarcheology of the Lower Mississippi Valley and Trans-Mississippi South
sources.note: Arkansas Archeological Survey Research Series 37, chapter 9, printed pages 255 to 256: exchange at Arkansas Post, regional products, and a 1775 list of trade or gift goods intended for Quapaw recipients.

sources.title: Arkansas Archeological Survey, Lesson Five: Gathering, Gardening, and Agriculture
sources.note: Section on the colonial era: abundant regional game, trade networks, and the 1686 arrangement between Quapaw people and Henri de Tonti to exchange French goods for beaver and deer furs at Arkansas Post.
